headline.main: World Order Under Attack: Defend International Law against Putin and Trump!
headline.social: World Order Under Attack: Defend International Law against Putin and Trump!

intro: Germany should take on a leadership role in defending the international legal order against attacks from Russia and, now, the United States. That also means that Friedrich Merz must rescind his invitation to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
text:
On the third anniversary of Russia’s full invasion of Ukraine, the U.S. voted in the United Nations against calling the Russian Federation the aggressor. U.S. President Donald Trump has not excluded the possibility of his country using force to take ownership of Greenland and the Panama Canal. Trump has also cast a covetous eye toward the Gaza Strip. He envisions transforming the coastal region into a vast holiday resort following the "voluntary” resettlement of the 2 million Palestinians who live there.
These signals from Washington are coming during a period of sustained uncertainty about the future of the international legal order. Russian President Vladimir Putin attacked this order head on with his aggression against Ukraine, an act that quickly triggered the deployment of the entire architecture of international law, including a warrant for Putin’s arrest from the International Criminal Court. Only the United Nations Security Council remained paralyzed because of veto powers China and Russia.
Now, though, the United States is rapidly backing away from the basic principles of the current international legal order. China, in particular, which has demonstrated a recent zealousness in testing the boundaries of international law in the South China Sea and with regard to the status of Taiwan, will likely be considering whether it should follow Washington’s example.
Given these developments, many have suggested that we are currently witnessing a shift to a new world order in which the law of the jungle is taking over from prevailing international law. This view, however, fails to appreciate the resilience of law’s inherent logic, expressed not least in those rules that govern the development and retrogression of the international legal order. In most cases, states can unilaterally withdraw from international treaties. This does not, however, apply to the norms of universal international law.
Customary international law, the core of which includes the prohibition of the use of violence and annexation, arises from a consistent practice by a sufficient number of states combined with a corresponding legal conviction. And that is also the only path to repealing or changing it.
As such, universal international law has, in the past, repeatedly been able to assert its normativity across longer time periods even in the face of seemingly overwhelming realpolitik challenges. Russia and the United States are thus not able to abruptly dismantle the foundations of the current international legal order even with their parallel renunciations of compliance – unless, that is, most remaining nations fall in line behind the imperial aspirations of these two powers by abandoning their own convictions that universal international law remains in place. The political scientist Herfried Münkler recently published a plea for exactly that form of defeatism in the German daily Süddeutsche Zeitung, declaring international law to be "completely uninteresting.” Yet kowtowing to Putin and Trump by abandoning international law in such a manner would be as short-sighted as it would be harmful.
The universal legal order, with its institutions that have been successively established since 1945, is imbued with the immeasurable pain caused by the injustice of wars of aggression, genocide and crimes against humanity. Furthermore, it is only the prohibition of aggression and annexation combined with the commitment to international norms that provides the foundation of trust, which promotes the long-term, stable cooperation that is in the interest of all states and creates the conditions under which global challenges can be overcome. Beyond that, it is unclear for how long Russia and the U.S. will continue to pursue a foreign policy strategy reduced to pure power politics – such that a strategy of "hibernation” for international law may be necessary in relation to those two states until this cold snap comes to an end.
Thus, instead of succumbing to paralysis as far as international legal policy is concerned, European Union member states should not hesitate to take on the role of guardian of universal international law together with other Western countries like Australia, the United Kingdom, Canada and New Zealand along with as many states from the Global South as possible. In no way would such a role contradict the long overdue realization that European Union member states must quickly develop the military capabilities necessary for defending themselves. In international politics, military power and adherence to international law are just as little inconsistent as are state power and domestic legal peace. The deployment of protective military power can serve to underpin the authority of international law. The danger of a "peace” deal being imposed on Ukraine with little regard to international law would be far less today had European military assistance for the country – which has been the target of an unlawful use of force since 2014 – not consistently been too little and too late.
A Contradictory Trend
European Union member states would also be well advised to not just defend the fundamental inter-state norms, such as the prohibition of violent aggression and annexation, but also to continue advocating for an international community constituted by individual countries as its central pillars, but which also supersedes those individual countries by enlisting them for the protection of civilian populations from genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. This concept, which has found its institutional expression in the bodies established for the protection of universal human rights and in the establishment of the International Criminal Court, has been facing significant pressure for some time.
China and Russia, in particular, have repeatedly – and prominently, in their 2016 joint declaration on the "promotion of international law” – indicated their firm intention to re-empower national sovereignty in the face of cosmopolitan trends that have been particularly pronounced since the 1990s. But here, too, a noteworthy contradictory trend has become apparent, expressed particularly incisively in the advisory opinion on the Middle East conflict issued last year by the International Court of Justice at the request of the United Nations General Assembly. With regard to Israel’s actions in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, the court didn’t just reaffirm the prohibition against annexing foreign territory rooted in international law, but it also strongly reprimanded Israel for violating the human rights of Palestinians in the occupied territories through systematic discrimination.
Countries in Africa and Latin America are particularly supportive of this trend – yet another reason why it would make sense for European Union member states to establish an alliance including as many countries from these two regions as possible to protect universal international law. Should Asian countries also wish to join, all the better. It would be inaccurate, of course, to claim universal harmony between the European Union and countries belonging to the Global South when it comes to international law. There are significant differences between the two sides on the scope of the right to self-defense under international law, for example, or the universal human rights minimum. Furthermore, the recent escalation of the Middle East conflict has led to renewed claims that Western applications of international law are rife with double standards.
Still, now would be the time to grab the initiative and launch a comprehensive dialogue on international law. This does not require granting the countries of the Global South saint status for their criticism of the West. What is needed is a dialogue at eye level, complete with European self-criticism regarding its own past violations of international law in addition to the realization that a universal international legal community leaves considerable room for pluralism not only when it comes to the form of government but also in human rights.
Beneficiary Putin
Two current international law policy initiatives could promote the urgently needed debate in defense of universal international law. Numerous countries from all regions of the world have thrown their support behind the establishment of a diplomatic conference for the adoption of an intergovernmental convention to prevent and punish crimes against humanity, which would act as a meaningful supplement to the venerable 1948 Genocide Convention. In addition, the state parties to the International Criminal Court will convene in July of this year for a special meeting to close a gaping loophole in the ICC’s founding treaty with regard to the prosecution of the crime of aggression stemming from the much higher hurdles to investigation than exist for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. The most prominent beneficiary of this loophole is Vladimir Putin.
In their negotiations aimed at forming a governing coalition in Berlin, German conservatives and Social Democrats should establish a framework such that their government can play a leadership role in the challenging task of safeguarding universal international law. Germany’s chancellor-in-waiting Friedrich Merz is called upon to recant his pledge to invite Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – against whom the International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant – to Germany and guarantee him free passage. Such an explicit disavowal of compliance with the first permanent international criminal court in legal history – a body established with the help of a decisive contribution from a Germany that has learned from its own responsibility for the most serious injustices imaginable – would be diametrically opposed to the task of protecting universal international law and its institutions.
